conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in because your INR was low and you had a fall yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I fell off my horse—landed hard on my back. My head snapped down but I didn’t lose consciousness. They did a CT at the outside ER and said no bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your INR was 1.7 when you got here. Because you have a mechanical mitral valve, we need your INR to stay above 3.0 for safety. That’s why we’re admitting you—to bridge with heparin until the warfarin catches up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve been on warfarin for years. Why did it drop this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not entirely sure yet. Sometimes changes in diet, fluid intake, or other meds can affect it. We’ll monitor closely and adjust your dose before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been eating less since the fall—my back and side really hurt. I’ve been taking tramadol and gabapentin like usual, but it’s not helping much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll reassess your pain and see what we can safely add. Given your kidney disease, some pain meds aren’t safe, but we’ll find a balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your INR is still low at 2.0. We’ve started IV heparin to protect your valve while we adjust the warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the heparin going to make me bleed? I’m on anticoagulants already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your blood work closely to avoid that. The heparin is temporary—just until your INR comes up safely with warfarin. We’ll check it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My back pain is still bothering me—can we try something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can try a small dose of oral dilaudid, but we have to be very careful. With your kidney function, it can build up and affect your breathing or alertness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. I guess I’d rather be a little uncomfortable than risk something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you a low dose of dilaudid earlier. The nurse mentioned you became very drowsy and your breathing slowed. We gave narcan to reverse it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember that… I just felt really out of it. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not uncommon in patients with kidney disease. The medication wasn’t clearing from your system, so it built up. We’ll avoid that med now and stick to safer options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad you caught it. Can we add something else for pain? Maybe more acetaminophen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can safely add acetaminophen. We’ll start 1000 mg every 8 hours. It’s safer for your kidneys and won’t affect your breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had another episode of drowsiness last night after another dose. We gave narcan again. A CT of your head was done to rule out any bleeding—good news, it’s normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another one? I didn’t realize… So it’s definitely the medication, not a brain injury?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the CT shows no bleeding or injury. Your confusion and drowsiness are most likely from the dilaudid not clearing. We’ve stopped it completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved. I was worried something was really wrong with my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were too, given your anticoagulation. But now we know it’s a medication effect. We’ll keep you on acetaminophen, tramadol, and gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is still impaired. You received dialysis yesterday, and we’ll continue your immunosuppressants and other ESRD meds as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My peritoneal catheter isn’t working well yet, is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not fully, no. It’s new, so it may take time. For now, we’re using your tunneled HD catheter for dialysis. We’ll follow up with your transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 3.2—finally in the target range. We’re stopping the heparin and continuing warfarin at 5 mg daily for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good! So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost. We want to see one more INR to confirm it stays stable. And we need to make sure your pain is manageable at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m doing better with the new pain meds. Still sore, but I can move around with my walker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest INR is 3.5—perfect. We’ll switch you to warfarin 2 mg daily to avoid it going too high, especially if your appetite stays low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why lower the dose if it’s finally in range?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your intake has been poor, and when you eat less, warfarin can become stronger. Lowering the dose helps prevent it from going too high once you’re home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ll be more careful with my diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two clear head CTs, your mental status is normal, and your pain is controlled. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I need help at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your recent fall and ongoing pain, we recommend a home health aide for a few days. We’ll help you apply for that service.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I don’t want to fall again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your labs are stable, you’re walking independently, and your INR is at 3.5. We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take warfarin 2 mg every night. Check your INR tomorrow and call the coagulation clinic with the result. Continue your pain meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try the acetaminophen first. If it’s not enough, call your PCP. We’ll also suggest a pain management consult if it continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I’ll follow up with my transplant team about the PD catheter too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your discharge instructions are ready, and the home health aide will contact you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better and safer now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: warfarin 2 mg tonight, INR test tomorrow, and call the coagulation clinic. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And no more horseback riding for a while!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart plan. Let’s get you healed first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re doing well. Take it easy, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and meds shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep an eye on the abrasion on your leg. Keep it clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been doing that. It’s not infected, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection. Just keep it covered and monitor for redness or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll see you in follow-up if needed. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you with discharge soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care and get some rest.
